title: The Wheel of Fortune: Adjusting as Circumstances Change

quickTake.upright: Things are turning. Opportunities and uncertainty arrive together; timely adjustment helps.
quickTake.reversed: Change is not keeping your pace. Steady yourself, then see which step you can alter.

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: Things are turning. Opportunities and uncertainty arrive together; timely adjustment helps.

Reversed in a sentence: Change is not keeping your pace. Steady yourself, then see which step you can alter.

Some changes arrive faster than a plan can accommodate. The Wheel of Fortune draws attention to timing, cycles, and the response you can still choose now.

sections.title: Follow the Wheel Around, Then Look at the Corners
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A large orange wheel occupies the center amid blue sky and clouds. Several concentric rings divide its face, with spokes extending from the center. Latin and Hebrew letters appear on the outer ring, and other symbols on an inner one. A blue sphinx sits at the top holding a sword in its forelimbs. A yellow serpent-shaped body descends on the left, while a red, long-snouted figure with a human body and animal head rises along the lower-right rim.

A winged figure occupies each corner: human at upper left, eagle at upper right, ox at lower left, lion at lower right, each with a book before it. The rim's curves and bodies at the sides suggest motion, while the corners frame the composition steadily. No one is turning a handle, and no ordinary person single-handedly controls the whole scene. [View the card image used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_10_Wheel_of_Fortune.jpg)

Do not rush to guess the wheel's direction: a still card does not tell us where the next turn will stop. The changing impression at the rim and steadiness of the book-bearing corner figures can help distinguish external fluctuations from practices you can maintain. The descending serpent and ascending figure also do not mean a particular real person is destined to rise or fall. Letters and symbols from different traditions require historical sources to explain them; their order cannot justify invented winning numbers. A more practical modern question is: Which conditions have changed, and which arrangements that worked before can still be kept?

sections.title: Blended Symbols Do Not Prove an Egyptian Origin
sections.bodyMarkdown: Waite says he adopted and adjusted Éliphas Lévi's conception, connects the corner figures with the four living creatures of Ezekiel, associates the wheel with life's flux, and makes the sphinx represent balance within it. He explicitly states that using Egyptian symbols does not assert an Egyptian origin for tarot. The mixed imagery belongs to this particular symbolic arrangement. [Waite, Part II, X](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar10.htm)

sections.title: Upright: Notice the Opening and Leave Some Margin
sections.bodyMarkdown:
This site reads upright as changing conditions: a previously blocked path may open, and a familiar method may need updating. You can take an opportunity while checking its time limit, participation requirements, and actual cost. Moving with circumstances means acting on new information, not treating every coincidence as an instruction.

The wheel turns, and existing progress still needs maintenance. When a collaboration has just attracted attention, organizing processes and capacity promptly is more practical than assuming the interest will last forever.

sections.title: Reversed: Distinguish Setbacks, Excess, and Repetition
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Modern readers often use reversal to think about blockage, repetition, or resistance to change. This article follows that direction to practice adaptability without passing it off as Waite's original wording: his reversed entry instead lists increase, abundance, and excess. Another worthwhile question therefore remains: Are so many opportunities arriving that your resources cannot accommodate them? [Waite, Part III, §3, entry 10](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pkt0303.htm)

First locate the real change. Has an external condition delayed the schedule, or do you repeat an old approach whenever feedback arrives? The former needs buffers and alternatives; the latter may need a different method. They are not the same kind of “bad luck.”

sections.title: Distinguishing Related Meanings
sections.bodyMarkdown: The Wheel of Fortune and Chariot may both appear in questions about progressing a plan. The Chariot tends to ask how to concentrate forces that can be organized; the Wheel better identifies external conditions, timing, and recurring patterns. Unlike the Tower, change need not mean an abrupt break in an existing structure. It might simply be more registrations, a seasonal transition, or changed availability. Reversal especially need not always mean misfortune: Waite's reversed list includes increase and excess. A sudden increase in opportunities can reveal insufficient capacity. Judgment must return to actual changes rather than the card's orientation alone.

sections.title: An Exhibition Space Opens Unexpectedly: How to Take the Opportunity
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Zhouqing asks, “The exhibition wall I've waited ages for has suddenly become free for two weeks. Should I take it?”

Known facts: The community venue has confirmed the dates. She has six finished works that could make a small exhibition. The originally planned twelve are not finished, and she cannot substantially increase production time over these two weeks. She draws the upright Wheel of Fortune in the external-conditions position.

The turning wheel suits an opening that has genuinely appeared; the stable corner composition reminds her to keep her capacity boundaries. Upright does not require taking every opportunity, still less guarantee a career turning point. Six existing works are enough to discuss a smaller complete proposal. The key is fitting the scale to real conditions rather than hastily making up numbers to match the original vision.

Another possibility: If the dates are merely verbal speculation and venue requirements are unconfirmed, she should not invest in production on the premise that “the opportunity has arrived.” If six works cannot form a coherent exhibition, waiting is also an option. An opening does not automatically create readiness.

A practical next step: Confirm conditions of use and installation time, draft a one-page proposal limited to six works, and assess whether labels and installation can be completed on time. Leave unfinished work for another round. Accept or decline politely according to the actual burden, rather than fear of missing a destined moment.

sections.title: Taking Every Order During Quiet Periods, Then Missing Deadlines Again
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Ruohang asks, “Why do my handmade orders swing between busy and quiet, with frequent delays?”

Known facts: Whenever he has free time, he opens many custom-order slots, closing them only after production slows. Customers have different expectations, and promised dates do not include material-delivery time. Inquiries have recently increased again. He draws the reversed Wheel of Fortune in the recurring-pattern position.

Reversal here can mean excess and an unbalanced cycle, without attributing it to bad luck. External demand does fluctuate, but order limits and the way he makes promises are adjustable. The wheel's rim helps reveal “finish the rush, open too many slots, delay again,” while the steady corners can become consistent rules, avoiding estimates of an entire month based on one moment's spare time.

Another possibility: If the main delay comes from a single uncontrollable supply interruption, distinguish that rather than attributing every consequence to personal planning failure. If new inquiries have not become orders, do not assume capacity has already been exceeded.

A practical next step: Recalculate capacity from actual hours on the last three orders, allow buffers for materials and communication, and publish a clear production timeframe. Offer a waiting list when inquiries exceed capacity rather than immediately promising delivery. After one cycle, see whether delays have decreased, then adjust capacity.

sections.title: Practice: Leave a Way to Respond to Change
sections.bodyMarkdown: Make three columns: conditions that have changed, actions I can adjust, and things currently outside my control. Choose one small action for today only from the second column and write a backup plan. A few days later, review what actually happened rather than looking only for coincidences that fit the card.

sections.title: A Common Misreading
sections.bodyMarkdown: The Wheel of Fortune does not guarantee approaching good luck or decree that bad events must repeat. Its most useful question is: Now that circumstances have changed, am I still using an expired plan?

The wheel turns, and existing progress still needs maintenance. When a collaboration has just attracted attention, organizing processes and capacity promptly is more practical than assuming the interest will last forever.

## Distinguishing Related Meanings

The Wheel of Fortune and Chariot may both appear in questions about progressing a plan. The Chariot tends to ask how to concentrate forces that can be organized; the Wheel better identifies external conditions, timing, and recurring patterns. Unlike the Tower, change need not mean an abrupt break in an existing structure. It might simply be more registrations, a seasonal transition, or changed availability. Reversal especially need not always mean misfortune: Waite's reversed list includes increase and excess. A sudden increase in opportunities can reveal insufficient capacity. Judgment must return to actual changes rather than the card's orientation alone.

## An Exhibition Space Opens Unexpectedly: How to Take the Opportunity

Make three columns: conditions that have changed, actions I can adjust, and things currently outside my control. Choose one small action for today only from the second column and write a backup plan.
